newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli finance chief says inflation down, not out.
newsitem.headline: Israeli finance chief says inflation down, not out.

text.p: Israel's finance minister said on Monday he was encouraged by the Jewish state's falling inflation but was not sure the trend would continue.
"Inflation in the last eight months was low -- less than seven percent in annual terms. We haven't seen such figures since 1970," said Dan Meridor, appointed finance minister last June.
"Am I sure it will continue in this way? No," he told a conference of tax advisers in Jerusalem.
Meridor said the inflation rate was being forced down by the Bank of Israel's restrictive monetary policy that has kept interest rates high and prevented the shekel from depreciating.

Israel's 1996 inflation rate was 10.6 percent but in the second half of the year the annualised rate fell to less than seven percent despite a widening budget deficit of nearly five percent of gross domestic product.
The Bank of Israel says that was due to its tough monetary line but as Meridor indicated, a strong shekel due to high interest rates was a key factor in taming inflation.
Meridor said he was concerned about January's deficit, which reached 1.28 billion shekels ($383 million), and would consider making adjustments if the trend continued.

"It concerned us on the income side, mainly on the side of indirect taxes, on customs...We will follow things in the coming month and the one after that and we'll decide if an adjustment needs to be made in the expenditures," he said.
This year's budget binds the government to keep the deficit to 2.8 percent of GDP this year.
